1:
The woe sounds strange, and Henry says so: we are ready to think happy those at ease, who neither feel trouble nor fear any, who lie soft and warm and lay nothing to heart; those who do well for their bodies are looked on as doing well for themselves. Gill guards the point from the other side, since to be in easy circumstances is not criminal but a blessing of providence; the woe falls on the rich in Zion when they have nothing but temporal riches, trust in them, consume them on their lusts, remain unconcerned at the troubles of others and give no thought to their own future state. Wesley reduces the charge to a line: they neither fear nor believe the threatened judgments of God. Calvin makes it more precise. The prophet is not, as many suppose, reproving luxury and pride only; the fact in their case is that they were not awakened by the judgments of God, and while he severely punished the people the chief men remained heedlessly in their own dregs. It is not an evil thing, he says, when a man quietly enjoys his leisure; the fault is to be unmoved when the Lord openly shows himself displeased, and to indulge oneself the more in pleasures, which is to provoke him as it were designedly.

Calvin explains why the powerful feel a public calamity so little. When the Lord afflicts a country with war or famine, the rich make great gain of such evils and abuse the scourges of God: merchants grow rich in the midst of wars, because those who carry on war must borrow, and peasants and mechanics must borrow to pay their taxes and accept unjust conditions in order to live. Those in favour at court make more gain in war and famine than in peace, since when peace flourishes the state of things is more equable, but when the poor are burdened the rest grow fat. The chief men ought to have humbled themselves when they saw God incensed, and instead made themselves drunk with pleasure.

Why the two cities are named together lies in their repute. Henry has those in Zion thinking that honour and protection enough, since it was a strong city fortified by nature and art, a royal city where the thrones of the house of David were set, and above all the holy city, so they never doubted the sanctuary of God would be a sanctuary to them; many, he adds, are rocked asleep in carnal security by church privileges. Those in the other city trusted a hill that was not holy, because it was the metropolis of a potent kingdom and perhaps the headquarters of its religion, so that in time it came into as good repute as the holy hill. Wesley divides the two the same way, one standing for the kingdom of the two tribes and the other for the strength of the ten, both accounted chief cities of that part of the world. Ellicott presses the grammar of the second clause, since the word for trust is a participle and the parallelism calls for the confident dwellers in the mountain of Samaria; by these he understands the upper luxurious classes, and by the chief of the first of nations the rulers, to whom the nation came up for judgment, and who are now summoned to hear the rebuke of the divine Judge. Clarke would change a letter, reading a word meaning to lean confidently rather than to dwell at ease, which makes the first clause agree better with the second: they leaned on Zion, supposing that notwithstanding their iniquities they should be saved for its sake. Failing that, he takes those at ease for men who have no concern about the threatened judgments, and reports a third conjecture, that the words are a summons to those who despise Zion.
2:
Whether the three cities are named as ruins or as rivals is the question. Wesley takes them all as warnings: the second was head of the Syrian kingdom, lately overthrown, a fresh instance of the indignation of God against secure sinners, and the third the chief city of the Philistines, wasted a few years before; by these they should learn to amend their ways or expect to perish in them. Clarke reads it the same way: they have no more reason to expect exemption from the consequences of their sins than those cities had, and since these have been punished so shall they be; why then trust in gods that could not save their own cities? Gill supplies the antiquity of the first, a city in the land of Shinar as early as the days of Nimrod, which he thinks had probably been lately taken by the king of Assyria. Calvin agrees that they are set up as examples and calls the method a singular favour, since God could justly punish us as soon as we transgress and instead teaches us at the expense of others; these cities were evidences of his wrath, by which the people might learn not to rest on their wealth or rely on their fortresses, for as he had destroyed strongholds that seemed impregnable he could cut off their own whenever he pleased.

Two readings are set aside. Calvin knows a rendering that makes the question negative, whether these places are not better than your kingdoms, and says it is not consistent with the words of the prophet; and a second, in which the blessings of God are compared, as though he had dealt more liberally with this people than with their neighbours, which he notes most interpreters accept. Keil and Delitzsch say the double question requires a negative answer: the princes are to see that these cities are not better off than the two kingdoms and that their territory is no larger. They add the objection that tells against the reading by ruin, that the words evidently cannot apply to cities already destroyed. Ellicott presses the same difficulty from history, since we have no reason to believe the Assyrian power had yet destroyed the importance of these places, though the prophet may have thought that issue imminent; the third, the home of Goliath, had probably lost its importance already.

On putting far away the evil day they agree, and illustrate differently. Gill takes the day as that of the captivity, which they put out of their thoughts and supposed at a great distance; and he draws the parallel that some men put far from them the day of death, which to a good man is better than the day of his birth but to a wicked man is terrible, so that he will not think of it lest it dampen his carnal joys. Clarke turns the halves of the verse against each other: they bring their iniquities nearer and still suppose their punishment further off. Ellicott has them clinging closer to their habits of defrauding the poor at the seat of judgment; Keil and Delitzsch note that the verb means not to put the day far away but to regard it as far off. Calvin restricts the charge to the chiefs, the judges and counsellors in both kingdoms, and gives it a picture: you seek a fever by intemperance and then drive the thought away, as drunken men do who, when a physician warns them against excess, ridicule his forebodings and ask whether a fever will seize on them, who are wholly free from fever. Such are the ungodly, who provoke the wrath of God designedly and scorn every threatening as though some privilege made them safe; and they drew near the throne of iniquity when the judges strengthened themselves in their tyranny and took liberty to steal, to rob and to oppress.
4:
The beds are described before they are judged. Gill takes them as made of ivory, or inlaid or covered with it, and thinks it not improbable that some were wholly of ivory, since an ancient writer reports a people whose beds were entirely so; he adds that an old paraphrase has Joseph laying his father on a bed of ivory, though its Latin interpreters render the word a cedar bed while two later scholars take it for ivory. Clarke allows that they may be either sofas to recline on at table or beds to sleep on, ornamented among the ancients with inlaid ivory, and suggests that those inlaid with mother-of-pearl may be meant; he infers great luxury and consequently abundance of riches in a kingdom that had long enjoyed peace, and says the description is that of an Asiatic court even in his own day. Ellicott says only that the beds were inlaid with the material, and Wesley that out of laziness or luxury they lay themselves down to rest and eat the very best in all the flock.

Calvin will not let the charge rest on luxury as such. Luxury is not simply reprehended here, he says, as some incorrectly think; the prophet upbraids them for setting up an iron neck against the judgments of God and trifling with him while he was endeavouring to lead them by degrees to repentance. To use an ivory bed was not in itself bad, except that excess is always to be condemned, since every desire for present things which exceeds moderation is justly reprehensible; but a man might use such a bed and still be willing to lie on the ground. He adds a piece of history: ivory was then abundant in the east, and Italy did not know what it was to use a bed of ivory until a certain conquest, after which she used ivory beds freely, so that luxury broke down her courage. It may be that ivory was not costly in that country either, and such beds might be used without blame; what the prophet regards is the misery around them.

The music is described and then disputed. Gill explains the instrument as one of twelve cords giving twelve sounds, stricken with the fingers, and the chanting as a quivering of the voice raised and lowered to match it, the word signifying to observe the divisions and distinctions of notes by the modulation of the voice. Ellicott says the Hebrew word occurs only here and is best rendered prattle, or jabber, and takes the comparison with David as ironical, since he made his instruments to please the Lord and these princes theirs to please themselves. Keil and Delitzsch have them prattling to the tune of the harp and taking such pleasure in it that they invent new kinds of playing and singing. Calvin derives the word from dividing, and reports the explanation that traces it to the clusters left after a vintage, which stand here and there rather than thick together, so that the participle is used of dividing by marks, as music has its various notes; for unless there be a distinct variety in singing the sound would be confused. He then denies flatly that music is condemned: whoever thinks so is much deceived, as appears from the context, since the prophet never dealt so rigidly with the people but kept to one point, that they were destitute of common sense in not perceiving that God showed himself angry with them. The comparison with David, he adds, greatly aggravates their sin. Clarke takes the comparison the opposite way, holding that David was not authorised to introduce that multitude of musical instruments into divine worship, and that his conduct is here solemnly reprehended by the prophet. Wesley states the offence more simply, that in a time of deep mourning they entertain themselves with songs and musical instruments.
6:
The bowls are read for their size by most and for their price by one. Gill notes that the drinking was not in small cups but in large bowls, so that they might drink freely, even to drunkenness, and reports an alternative rendering that has them drinking in bowls of wine. Wesley says the vessels were not little ones but bowls, filled as full as they could hold, and that the design was to drink each other down. Ellicott takes the extent of their potations to be indicated by the fact that they drink not from wine-cups but from large bowls, in which the wine was probably mixed, and observes that the same word is used elsewhere for the sacrificial basons. Clarke turns the point the other way and suggests that perhaps the costliness of the vessels rather than the quantity drunk is what the prophet reprehends, since vessels of the most costly materials are still in use; and on the ointments he cites the price of one small box in the Gospel to show what such things could be worth. Calvin has the vessels either elegantly formed or precious, and knows a reading that supplies the word silver, but sees no need to regard anything as understood in the words.

Why anointing should be blamed at all is answered carefully. Calvin points out that anointing is not in itself sinful, having been used without blame by kings and others and practised upon Christ himself, so that the prophet must have something particular in view. What he meant to show, Calvin says, is that when God manifests tokens of his wrath nothing remains for men conscious of evil but to abstain humbly, like guilty persons, from all indulgences, so that by fasting and mourning they may excite his mercy; and because they had not done this the prophet expostulates with them. The same holds of the drinking, since they drank according to their usual custom when they ought to have betaken themselves to fasting and mourning, to sackcloth and ashes, and their madness was conspicuous in not forsaking their indulgences while God was manifesting his vengeance. Wesley notes only that in those hot countries anointing was much used, and that they were nothing affected with the calamities of their country. Ellicott would render the last clause that they are not sick at heart for the ruin of Joseph, and states the principle behind it, that self-indulgence is indifferent to the call of duty or danger.

The sentence turns on the word first. Gill has these men, the first and chief in the nation, who would not believe the day of captivity would come and gratified their senses of tasting, hearing and smelling with no compassion for their afflicted brethren, becoming the first whom the enemy lays hold on; he recalls that in a later deportation it was the royal family, the princes and nobles and chief tradesmen who went first. Ellicott puts it that they shall go into captivity at the head of the captives and the shout of the loungers shall cease, so that all their loud merriment comes to a sorry end. Wesley says simply that the feastings of the voluptuous shall cease, and Clarke draws a different comparison, that the northern kingdom shall be carried into captivity before the southern. Calvin makes the word a matter of divine reckoning: when there shall be an emigration these shall be first in order of time, since God has spared them and they have abused his forbearance, so that they are to be the forerunners of the rest and his rigour begins with them, because he has lost all his labour in attempting kindly to call them to repentance. They lie down and stretch themselves on their couches, Calvin adds, and think they can escape punishment while they repose quietly on their beds; but mourning shall come to them.
8:
The oath is noticed for its form. Gill says God swears by himself because he could swear by no greater, which shows the certainty of the thing sworn to; Clarke renders the phrase literally as by his soul, his being, his existence; Ellicott takes it the same way, that he swears by his life because there is no greater, and notes that the standing formula of divine asseveration draws its force from the custom of swearing by the life of a monarch. Henry presses what the oath does to the sentence: the burden is bound on by the almighty hand which none can resist, and bound with an oath that puts the sentence past revocation, so that the case is dreadful of those whose ruin God himself has sworn.

What the excellency is divides the voices. Wesley takes it for all that the seed of Jacob accounts a glory to them, all their external privileges and worship. Henry specifies it further, all that they are proud of and value themselves upon: their visible church membership and its privileges, their temple, altar and priesthood, which were more than anything the excellencies of Jacob until they were profaned by sin. God abhors, he says, that form of godliness which hypocrites keep up while they abhor the power of it; and any creature we take such complacency in as to make it a rival with God is thereby made abominable to him. If he abhors their temple for its iniquity, he adds, it is no marvel that he hates their palaces for the injustice found in them, since he hates the palaces of sinners for the wickedness of those who dwell there. Ellicott finds something narrower in the sanctuary: the unchangeable being of the supreme Monarch stands contrasted with a false and futile glory, and from the context he infers that the splendid shrine of Samaria, with its unacceptable offerings and calf-worship, is meant, the coming destruction of buildings great and small lending colour to the reading.

Calvin makes the word itself the question. The Hebrew, he says, means both pride and excellency, but here it is taken in a good sense, as in other places where it is applied to God himself; the gifts of God always deserve praise, so the prophet is not inveighing against pride but showing that the people were deceived, since they set up their excellency against God as though they were thereby exempt from punishment. God had now rejected an excellency which was his own gift, because they had abused his benefits. The meaning, on his reading, is that there is no acceptance of persons before God, and the dignity conferred on this people was now of no moment, being a mere mask; it is as if the prophet had said, I will judge you as the common people and the heathen, for the dignity of which you are stripped is of no account with me. He insists twice that neither the palaces nor the excellency are named in a bad sense, and that what the prophet shows is that the blessings of God are no safeguard to the wicked.

The last clause is the consequence of the first. Henry draws it directly: if God abhors them he will deliver up the city with all that is in it into the hands of an enemy who will lay it waste, and those who are abhorred and abandoned of God are undone to all intents and purposes. Calvin puts the same in the words of the threat, that though they are now full of wealth God will empty them of all their abundance. Keil and Delitzsch treat the verse as the head of a longer passage, in which the threat is carried out through the deaths in the house down to the smiting of the great house into ruins and the small house into shivers.
9:
The number ten measures how complete the destruction is. Wesley reads it as a certain number put for an uncertain, men who have escaped the sword of the enemy and who, though they escape a while, shall not finally escape. Clarke says all shall be cut off, by the sword or by captivity or by famine. Calvin weighs the figure: in naming ten survivors the prophet intimates that a slaughter had gone before which had taken away half or some part of the family, and the point is that even these shall be taken together. It rarely happens, he observes, even in a direful pestilence, that so numerous a family entirely perishes; when three out of four, or six out of eight, are taken away, that is a diminution which usually terrifies men, but when ten are taken together and none is left, it is evidence of an awful vengeance. God would not take moderate vengeance now, since he had effected nothing by dealing moderately, and there was no remedy for so desperate a disease but to take away those who were incurable.

The burying is described as a scene of general death. Gill explains the uncle as the near kinsman to whom the right of inheritance belongs and with it the care of the funeral, and has him taking up the dead man himself because there is nobody left to employ, the mortality being universal, whether through a pestilence raging everywhere or, as one commentator supposes, through an earthquake that killed men by the fall of houses. Wesley adds what it displaces, that this office belonged to men who were paid for it, and that with none of these remaining the nearest survivor must carry the body on his shoulders; though the people mostly buried their dead, in some cases, such as a pestilence, they burned them, the bones being reserved for burial. Clarke reports an authority who takes the whole obscure verse for the effects of famine and pestilence during a siege, with the carcase burnt and the bones removed without funeral rites, solitude reigning in the house, and any survivor keeping silent lest he be plundered; he notes that burning the body and collecting the ashes into an urn was reckoned the most honourable burial.

Calvin reconstructs the scene more exactly than anyone. When an uncle comes to bury the dead, he says, it shows that unless neighbours performed the duty bodies would be left unburied, which never happened except in extreme devastation; and since the office was servile and usually left to hirelings, an uncle constrained to do it is proof of great confusion. On the second figure he adopts the rendering by burning, and explains why: bodies were usually carried out and burnt publicly, but one man, and an old man at that, could not carry out a body, so the uncle would burn his nephews within the house in order to have only the bones to carry, the burden being lighter. He rejects the reading that makes the kinsman a maternal uncle, since to mention two would imply that many men were still remaining, whereas one suits a place where men were so few.

The silence at the end is read as terror or despair. Calvin takes the man addressed to be in the next dwellings, Keil and Delitzsch in the hindermost corner of the house, with the answer that the name of the Lord is not to be invoked. Wesley makes the speaker call to anyone near the house out of which the bones are carried, asking whether any one is still living within, and reads the command to hold the tongue as a warning not to complain, lest the man be killed and all be rifled; the reason given, he says, is that it is too late to seek God, who is executing his immutable decree.
11:
The great house and the little house level ranks. Clarke says great and small shall equally suffer, with no distinction made and rich and poor falling together, since death has received his commission and will spare none; he quotes a Latin poet for the same sentiment, that pale death knocks with impartial foot at the cottages of the poor and the towers of kings. He offers a second, more local explanation, that the clause may refer to the houses of the poor in eastern countries, whose mud walls are full of clefts because the earth they are built of seldom adheres. Wesley divides the two strokes by size, great breaches in the palaces of great men and the cottages of the poor ruined by lesser ones, and takes the verse for the continued speech of the man who had care of the dead. Ellicott would read ruins for breaches and says the overthrow of all classes of the population is meant. Gill notes that the Lord has determined the judgment, and reports a commentator who paraphrases the command as a decree of earthquake.

Calvin adds two points. The verse confirms the sentence before it, that the common people as well as the chiefs trusted in vain in their quiet state. By the word commands, he says, the prophet means both that God had many reasons to destroy them and that their destruction depended on his sole will: though he send no ministers of vengeance and prepare no great forces, his word only, whenever it goes forth, will consume them all. On the word describing the greater ruin he prefers the sense of confusion, and explains the difference physically: when a cottage is overturned no great ruin is occasioned by its weight, the fragments falling one after another so that the whole comes down without violence, whereas the downfall of a great building is tremendous.

The horses on the rock are an image of wasted effort, and Clarke finds four in it. They could not run there at all, he says, being unshod, since shoeing with iron was not then known; if they did, it would be useless to their owner and hurtful to themselves; it would be as useless to plough there; and just as useless is it to put gall in the place of judgment. They have not only laboured in vain, he concludes, but have been oppressive to others, and for both they shall suffer. Gill puts the two questions as one: would any man be so weak as to propose a horse race upon rocks, where horse and rider might break their necks, or take oxen to plough where no impression can be made? As vain, he applies it, would it be to bring to repentance men given up to a hardness of heart like that of a rock. Wesley says in a line that if prophets exhort or advise it does no more good than running horses upon the precipices of rocks. Ellicott holds that the questions require a negative answer and show the conduct of the nation to be as senseless as the suppositions they contain: what should have insured the stability of the state had been turned into narcotic poison. On the plants he is precise: the word rendered gall is a poisonous plant of bitter taste, resembling stalks of grass and propagating so fast that it is hard to exterminate, while the word rendered hemlock is elsewhere rendered wormwood, which he says should have stood here. Calvin says interpreters misrepresent the verse, and reports three: some make the figures mean the people were unprofitable for anything good, as the proverb has the slothful ox wishing for the saddle and the horse to plough; others that the order of things was subverted, so that they had become monsters; others that the prophet complains of having lost all his labour, singing to the deaf.
13:
What the thing of nought is depends on what each thinks they boasted of. Clarke takes it of their idols, since an idol is nothing in the world, and Wesley of their victories, alliances and idols together. Ellicott refers it to the calf-worship, the idol Israel is glorying in, the idolatrous travesty of the Eternal which they call the excellency of Jacob. Gill runs through several: their wealth and riches, which are things that are not, because of their uncertainty; or any of the things of this world, its lusts and honours, human wisdom or strength, all of no worth and no continuance; or their idols; or their own works of righteousness, as with men of a pharisaical temper. He is careful with that last, since such works are something when done in obedience to the will of God and from right principles; they are things of nought only as a ground of rejoicing. Calvin takes the phrase of the fallacies by which they deceived not only others but themselves, since hypocrites do not merely pretend the name of God but lull themselves asleep with self-flatteries, arrogating the name of the Church and the empty title of adoption.

The horns are agreed to be power, and the boast to be the point. Clarke explains that horns were the symbols of power, so the claim is to have arrived at power and dignity by their own strength, and quotes a Latin poet for the idiom, that wine repairs our strength and furnishes the poor with horns, since at such times men think themselves as great as the greatest. Wesley says they have raised themselves to greatness by their wisdom and courage. Ellicott glosses the horns as instruments of resistance and aggression, and sets the boast against the record: the sacred historian takes quite a different view of the success of the king under whom these victories were won, whereas these boasters reckoned it due to their own ingenuity; he compares the language put into the mouth of a Pharaoh, that the river is his own and he made it for himself.

The nation raised up is identified alike by all. Gill names the Assyrian nation under its king, who invaded the land, came up to Samaria and after a three years siege carried the people captive into foreign lands. Clarke names three Assyrian kings who subdued them at various times and at last carried them away in the days of the last king to reign in Samaria, and identifies the river of the wilderness as the stream that empties into the sea near Gaza. Wesley marks the two limits as a city of Syria bordering Israel to the north-east and the south-western parts of the land, so the whole country shall be destroyed. Ellicott makes the same measurement and draws the irony out: the entire limits of the kingdom after the victories of the king just alluded to were identical with the region here threatened with invasion, from the mouth of one valley to the wadi that formed the southern boundary of Moab, whose name appears elsewhere in a form implying a torrent of the poplars.

Calvin ends on a large country turned into a trap. He has no doubt the Assyrians are meant, and expresses how dreadful that war would be: though their land was large and spacious, and so had many outlets, the prophet shows there would be straits everywhere once the Lord raised up that nation. He notes that the Lord is again called the God of hosts for the reason given before, that they might understand the Assyrians were at his disposal and would stir up war whenever he gave the signal. The last word of the chapter, on his reading, is that once the Lord had armed them the most spacious places were made strait, so that no escape from death would be open.
